title: Namchi's Char Dham and Samdruptse: a visitor's guide
meta_description: Visit Namchi's Char Dham on Solophok and the 135 ft Guru Padmasambhava at Samdruptse: what they are, how to plan the day, fees, timing and nearby stops.
summary: Namchi, the headquarters of South Sikkim, has two giant statues on facing hills: a 135 ft Guru Padmasambhava at Samdruptse, completed in 2004, and a 108 ft Shiva at Siddhesvara Dham, the Char Dham complex on Solophok. Both are easy half-day visits from Namchi, Ravangla or Temi and cost little to enter.

sections.heading: Namchi, the sky-high town
paras: Namchi means 'sky high' in Sikkimese, a fair name for a town that sits on a ridge at about 1,300–1,500 m with hills rising on every side. It is the headquarters of Namchi district, the old South District, and a busy, practical place with banks, schools, a large new district hospital and the Bhaichung Stadium, named after Sikkim's best-known footballer. For travellers it is the gateway to the south: Ravangla, Temi and Tendong are each about an hour away.

Namchi also has a place in the darker pages of Sikkim's history. Wikipedia's account of the town records that after the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, was murdered in 1716, his half-sister Pende Ongmu, who had arranged the killing, was caught and executed at Namchi. Today the town is better known for something quite different: two of the largest religious statues in the eastern Himalaya, one Buddhist and one Hindu, facing each other across the valley.

sections.heading: Samdruptse and Guru Padmasambhava
paras: On Samdruptse hill, a few kilometres above Namchi, a statue of Guru Padmasambhava, Guru Rinpoche, rises 135 ft (about 41 m). It was completed in February 2004. Padmasambhava is the 8th-century master who, in Buddhist tradition, brought tantric Buddhism to Tibet and blessed the hidden valleys of Sikkim; the Nyingma monasteries of West Sikkim all trace their lineage to him. On a clear day its copper and gold colours can be picked out from the Namchi ridge and from the road below.

The name Samdruptse is often translated as the 'wish-fulfilling hill', and local tradition holds that the hill is a sleeping volcano kept quiet by the prayers offered there; we pass that on as a local belief, not geology. A paved path climbs from the car park past prayer wheels to the statue's base, and on clear mornings you can see the snows of the Kangchenjunga range to the north and the Darjeeling hills to the south.

For Buddhist visitors the hill is a place of prayer, not just a viewpoint. Walk clockwise around the statue, spin the prayer wheels with your right hand, and do not sit with your feet pointing at the image. Butter lamps and incense are offered at the shrine below the statue. If you are lucky you will meet families from Namchi who come up on weekend mornings with flasks of tea and stay for hours.

sections.heading: Siddhesvara Dham, the Char Dham of Sikkim
paras: Across the valley on Solophok hill, about 5 km from Namchi, Siddhesvara Dham is a large Hindu pilgrimage complex built by the Sikkim government. At its centre stands a 108 ft (33 m) statue of Shiva, seated, with an 18 ft image of Kirateshwar, the form in which, in Hindu tradition, Shiva appeared to Arjuna as a hunter. Around it are replicas of the four dhams of India, Badrinath, Dwarka, Jagannath Puri and Rameswaram, and of the twelve jyotirlingas.

For pilgrims who cannot travel to all four corners of India, the complex offers a symbolic yatra in a single morning. That, more than the scale of the statues, is why so many families from Bengal, Bihar and beyond come here. Expect wide stairways, ramps, gardens and a steady stream of visitors, especially at weekends and during Shivratri and Shravan.

The complex is built to be walked as a circuit. You enter through a large gate, climb to the platform of the Shiva statue, then follow the paths that lead past each of the four dham replicas and the shrines of the jyotirlingas. Give yourself time: the full circuit is long, and there are benches and shaded spots along the way. Many pilgrims bring flowers, bel leaves and milk for the Shiva lingam; these are sold at stalls near the entrance at modest prices. Keep your ticket handy, since it may be checked at more than one point.

sections.heading: Planning the day
paras: Both sites fit comfortably into a half day with a car, or a full relaxed day with a stop at Temi Tea Garden or Namchi's Rock Garden. Go to Samdruptse early, when the light is best and the mountains are most likely to be clear, and to Char Dham afterwards. A local taxi for the two hills and back costs about ₹1,500–2,500, indicative 2026.
list: Start at Samdruptse by 8–9 am for the clearest view.
Char Dham has many steps; there are ramps, but older visitors should take it slowly.
Carry water and a light jacket; both hills are windy.
Leave shoes at the counters where asked, and dress modestly at both sites.

sections.heading: Tendong and the Lepcha flood story
paras: Above Damthang, on the road between Namchi and Ravangla, rises the long forested ridge of Tendong. In Lepcha tradition it is the hill that saved their ancestors when the Teesta and Rangeet flooded the land: the people climbed Tendong and the hill rose with the water to keep them safe. Every year on 8 August, a Sikkim state holiday, Lepcha families mark Tendong Lho Rumfaat, the 'prayer of the Tendong mountain', and many walk to the top, at about 2,600 m.
The Tendong walk takes roughly 3–4 hours up through forest and is best from October to April when the trail is dry. Go with a local guide, carry water and snacks, and start early.

sections.heading: Mamley and the oldest life in Sikkim
paras: Just outside Namchi, the Mamley Stromatolite Park protects rocks that record some of the oldest life in the region. Stromatolites are layered structures built up by mats of algae, here preserved in dolomite and limestone from the Proterozoic era, well over 500 million years ago. The Geological Survey of India declared the site a National Geological Monument in 2014. It is small and quiet, and worth half an hour for anyone curious about how these mountains were made.

sections.heading: Where to stay and how to get there
paras: Namchi is about 100 km and 3.5–4 hours from Siliguri, 78 km and 3 hours from Gangtok, and 27 km and an hour from Ravangla. Shared jeeps from Siliguri cost about ₹300–400 a seat, and from Ravangla about ₹80–120, indicative 2026. The town has plenty of mid-range hotels. For a quieter night, stay in Ravangla, where Mt. Narsing Village Resort and the hotels on Kewzing Road are well placed, or at Cherry Resort inside the Temi tea estate, and visit Namchi as a day trip. Check current status before you travel.

If you are travelling as a family of pilgrims from the plains, the simplest plan is two nights in Namchi itself: arrive by afternoon, see Char Dham at sunset, do Samdruptse the next morning, add Temi and Ravangla's Buddha Park in the afternoon, and leave on the third morning. A reserved car for the whole stay, including the round trip from Siliguri, costs roughly ₹11,000–14,000, indicative 2026, which is reasonable when shared by four or five people.

Budget travellers can do almost everything with local transport. Shared jeeps run from Namchi's central stand towards Damthang, Ravangla and Jorethang through the morning, and local taxis wait at the stand for short hops up to the two hills. Bargain politely and agree the waiting time before you set off.

faqs.q: What is the Char Dham in Namchi
faqs.a: Siddhesvara Dham, usually called Char Dham, is a Hindu pilgrimage complex on Solophok hill about 5 km from Namchi. It has a 108 ft seated Shiva, an 18 ft Kirateshwar image, and replicas of the four dhams, Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri and Rameswaram, as well as the twelve jyotirlingas, so pilgrims can make a symbolic yatra in one visit.

faqs.q: How tall is the Guru Padmasambhava statue at Samdruptse
faqs.a: It is 135 ft, about 41 m, tall, and stands on Samdruptse hill above Namchi. It was completed in February 2004. Guru Padmasambhava, or Guru Rinpoche, is the 8th-century master revered by the Nyingma monasteries of Sikkim. On clear mornings the Kangchenjunga range is visible from the hilltop.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Char Dham Namchi
faqs.a: Entry has been around ₹50–100 per person for Indian visitors, indicative for 2026, with separate rates for some facilities. Samdruptse charges a smaller fee, about ₹20–50. Fees are revised from time to time, so carry cash and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much time do I need for Namchi
faqs.a: Half a day covers Samdruptse and Char Dham by car. A full day lets you add the Rock Garden, the Mamley Stromatolite Park and Temi Tea Garden. Most visitors base themselves in Ravangla or Namchi for one night and see the south in a single relaxed day.

faqs.q: Is Namchi suitable for senior citizens
faqs.a: Yes, with some care. Both main sites have parking close to the entrance and paved paths. Char Dham has many steps, though ramps help, and Samdruptse has a short uphill walk. Take it slowly, carry water, and avoid the midday sun in May. Shared jeeps are cramped, so seniors are better off in a reserved car.

faqs.q: How do I reach Namchi from Siliguri
faqs.a: Namchi is about 100 km and 3.5–4 hours by road via Sevoke, Melli and Jorethang. Shared jeeps from the Siliguri stands cost about ₹300–400 a seat and SNT buses are cheaper; a reserved car costs about ₹4,000–5,000, indicative 2026. Leave in the morning. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see Kangchenjunga from Namchi
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days, best from Samdruptse hill and the higher parts of town, especially between October and February in the early morning. The view is more distant than from Pelling. By mid-morning in spring, haze often hides the range. In the monsoon months it is rarely visible.

It is the Lepcha festival of the Tendong mountain, held every year on 8 August, a state holiday in Sikkim. In Lepcha tradition Tendong hill, above Damthang near Namchi, saved their ancestors from a great flood. Families pray, build nine-stone models of the hill and many climb to the top.

faqs.q: Should I stay in Namchi or Ravangla
faqs.a: Ravangla is cooler and quieter and has the Buddha Park and Ralang Monastery nearby; Namchi is a busier town with more shops and transport. Many visitors stay in Ravangla and visit Namchi on a day trip, or stay at Temi between the two. Pilgrims focused on Char Dham may prefer Namchi itself.
